questions.stem: Explain any three methods of soil conservation practised in India.
questions.answer: Contour ploughing: ploughing along the contour lines slows the flow of water down the slopes. Terrace cultivation: steps are cut out on slopes to make terraces, which restrict erosion; the western and central Himalayas have well developed terrace farming. Strip cropping: large fields are divided into strips and strips of grass are left to grow between the crops, which breaks up the force of the wind. Shelter belts: rows of trees are planted to create shelter; they have helped stabilise sand dunes and the desert in western India.
valuePoints: Contour ploughing decelerates the flow of water down slopes
Terrace cultivation restricts erosion on slopes
Strip cropping breaks the force of the wind

questions.stem: Describe the main features of arid soils. What role does the kankar layer play in them?
questions.answer: Arid soils range from red to brown in colour, are generally sandy in texture and saline in nature; in some areas the salt content is so high that common salt is obtained by evaporating the water. Because of the dry climate and high temperature, evaporation is faster and the soil lacks humus and moisture. The lower horizons are occupied by kankar because calcium content increases downwards; this kankar layer restricts the infiltration of water. After proper irrigation these soils become cultivable, as in western Rajasthan.
valuePoints: Red to brown, sandy and saline
Lacks humus and moisture because of faster evaporation
Kankar in the lower horizons, due to calcium content increasing downwards, restricts infiltration of water

questions.stem: Alluvial soil is the most widely spread and important soil of India. Describe its distribution, composition, classification by age and fertility.
questions.answer: Distribution: the entire northern plains are made of alluvial soil deposited by the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra river systems; it extends into Rajasthan and Gujarat through a narrow corridor and is found in the eastern coastal plains, particularly the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Composition: it consists of various proportions of sand, silt and clay; particles are bigger inland towards the river valleys, and near the break of slope the soils are coarse, as in piedmont plains such as Duars, Chos and Terai. Age: old alluvium (bangar) has more kankar nodules; new alluvium (khadar) has more fine particles and is more fertile. Fertility: it contains adequate potash, phosphoric acid and lime, ideal for sugarcane, paddy, wheat and other cereal and pulse crops, so these regions are intensively cultivated and densely populated. Soils in drier areas are more alkaline and can be productive after proper treatment and irrigation.
valuePoints: Northern plains, deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; also Rajasthan–Gujarat corridor and eastern coastal deltas
Sand, silt and clay; coarse near the break of slope (Duars, Chos, Terai)
Bangar (old, more kankar) and khadar (new, finer, more fertile)
Rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime; suited to sugarcane, paddy, wheat, cereals and pulses
Intensively cultivated and densely populated; drier areas more alkaline

questions.stem: Explain how human activities have caused land degradation in different parts of India. Suggest measures to solve the problem.
questions.answer: Causes: Deforestation due to mining has caused severe land degradation in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha; abandoned mining sites leave deep scars and traces of over-burdening. Overgrazing is a main reason in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. Over-irrigation in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh causes waterlogging, increasing salinity and alkalinity in the soil. Mineral processing such as grinding limestone for cement and calcite and soapstone for ceramics produces dust that settles on land and retards the infiltration of water. Industrial effluents have become a major source of land and water pollution. Measures: afforestation and proper management of grazing; shelter belts, control on overgrazing and stabilising sand dunes with thorny bushes in arid areas; proper management of waste lands; control of mining activities; proper discharge and disposal of industrial effluents and wastes after treatment.

Overgrazing — Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra

Dust from mineral processing and industrial effluents

questions.passage: In June 1992, more than 100 heads of states met in Rio de Janeiro in Brazil for the first International Earth Summit. It was convened to address urgent problems of environmental protection and socio-economic development at the global level. The leaders signed the Declaration on Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity. The Rio Convention endorsed the global Forest Principles and adopted Agenda 21 for achieving sustainable development in the 21st century. Agenda 21 is an agenda to combat environmental damage, poverty and disease through global co-operation on common interests, mutual needs and shared responsibilities. One of its major objectives is that every local government should draw up its own local Agenda 21.

questions.stem: Describe how communities have conserved and protected forests and wildlife in India.
questions.answer: In Sariska Tiger Reserve, Rajasthan, villagers have fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act. The inhabitants of five villages in Alwar district of Rajasthan declared 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri', with their own rules which do not allow hunting, and protect the wildlife against outside encroachments. The Chipko movement in the Himalayas resisted deforestation in several areas and showed that community afforestation with indigenous species can be enormously successful. Farmers and citizens' groups like the Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya have shown that diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is possible and economically viable. Sacred groves have been left untouched by local people because of nature worship, and in and around Bishnoi villages in Rajasthan blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks are protected by the community. The Joint Forest Management programme involves local communities in restoring degraded forests.

questions.stem: Why was Project Tiger needed? Describe its aims and name any three tiger reserves of India with their states.
questions.answer: In 1973 the tiger population had dwindled to 1,827 from an estimated 55,000 at the turn of the century. The major threats were poaching for trade, shrinking habitat, depletion of prey base species and growing human population. The trade of tiger skins and the use of their bones in traditional medicines, especially in Asian countries, left the tiger on the verge of extinction. Since India and Nepal provide habitat to about two-thirds of the surviving tiger population in the world, they became prime targets for poaching and illegal trading. Project Tiger, launched in 1973, viewed tiger conservation not only as saving an endangered species but equally as a means of preserving biotypes of sizeable magnitude. Tiger reserves include Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand), Sunderbans National Park (West Bengal), Bandhavgarh National Park (Madhya Pradesh), Sariska Wildlife Sanctuary (Rajasthan), Manas Tiger Reserve (Assam) and Periyar Tiger Reserve (Kerala).

questions.passage: Nature worship is an age-old tribal belief based on the idea that all creations of nature have to be protected. Such beliefs have preserved several virgin forests in pristine form, called sacred groves — the forests of gods and goddesses. Local people leave these patches untouched, and any interference with them is banned. Some societies revere a particular tree: the Mundas and the Santhal of the Chota Nagpur region worship mahua and kadamba trees, while the tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship tamarind and mango trees during weddings. Troops of macaques and langurs are fed daily around many temples, and in and around Bishnoi villages in Rajasthan, herds of blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks live as part of the community and nobody harms them.

questions.stem: In recent years, multi-purpose projects and large dams have come under great scrutiny and opposition. Explain five reasons.
questions.answer: (1) Regulating and damming rivers affects their natural flow, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, resulting in rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for aquatic life. (2) Dams fragment rivers, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning. (3) Reservoirs created on floodplains submerge existing vegetation and soil, leading to their decomposition. (4) Dams built to control floods have triggered floods due to sedimentation and have mostly failed to control floods during excessive rainfall; flood plains are deprived of silt, a natural fertiliser, adding to land degradation. (5) Multi-purpose projects induced earthquakes, caused water-borne diseases and pests and pollution from excessive use of water. (6) Irrigation changed cropping patterns towards water-intensive commercial crops, causing salinisation of the soil.

questions.stem: Describe how rooftop rainwater harvesting through 'tankas' was carried out in the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan. Why is the practice declining?
questions.answer: In Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost all houses traditionally had underground tanks or tankas for storing drinking water; they could be as large as a big room. The tankas were built inside the main house or the courtyard and connected to the sloping roofs through a pipe; rain falling on the roof travelled down the pipe into the tanka. The first spell of rain was usually not collected, as it cleaned the roofs and pipes; water from later showers was collected. The water could be stored till the next rainfall, making it a reliable source of drinking water in summer when other sources dried up. This rainwater, called palar pani, is considered the purest form of natural water. Many houses built underground rooms beside the tanka to keep cool in summer. The practice is declining in western Rajasthan because plenty of water is available from the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal, though some houses keep tankas as they do not like the taste of tap water.

questions.passage: The Sardar Sarovar Dam has been built over the Narmada river in Gujarat. It is one of the largest water resource projects of India, covering four states — Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Rajasthan. The project is meant to meet the requirement of water in drought-prone and desert areas. It will provide irrigation to 18.45 lakh hectares of land, covering 3,112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. It will also irrigate 2,46,000 hectares in the desert districts of Barmer and Jalore in Rajasthan, and 37,500 hectares in the tribal hilly tract of Maharashtra through lift. About 75 per cent of the command area in Gujarat is drought prone, while the entire command in Rajasthan is drought prone.

questions.stem: Distinguish between intensive subsistence farming and commercial farming.
questions.answer: Intensive subsistence farming is practised in areas of high population pressure on land; it is labour-intensive and uses high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation for higher production; farmers take maximum output from limited land because the right of inheritance has made holdings uneconomical and there is no alternative livelihood. Commercial farming uses higher doses of modern inputs such as HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides to obtain higher productivity; its degree of commercialisation varies by region, e.g. rice is commercial in Haryana and Punjab but a subsistence crop in Odisha; plantation is one type of it.

questions.stem: Describe the institutional and technological reforms introduced by the Government of India to improve agriculture.
questions.answer: After Independence, collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari were given priority; land reform was the main focus of the First Five Year Plan, though implementation of the laws was lacking or lukewarm. In the 1960s and 1970s the Green Revolution based on package technology and the White Revolution (Operation Flood) were introduced, though these concentrated development in a few areas. In the 1980s and 1990s a comprehensive land development programme included both institutional and technical reforms: crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease; Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks giving loans at lower interest. The Kisan Credit Card and the Personal Accident Insurance Scheme were introduced; special weather bulletins and agricultural programmes were broadcast on radio and television; and the government announces minimum support price, remunerative and procurement prices for important crops to check exploitation by speculators and middlemen.

questions.stem: Compare rice and wheat in terms of their season, geographical conditions and main growing areas.
questions.answer: Rice: a kharif crop and the staple food of a majority of Indians; India is the second largest producer after China. It needs high temperature (above 25°C), high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm; in areas of less rainfall it is grown with irrigation. It is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, coastal areas and deltaic regions; canal irrigation and tubewells have made it possible in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan. Wheat: a rabi crop, the second most important cereal and the main food crop in the north and north-west. It needs a cool growing season, bright sunshine at ripening and 50 to 75 cm of annual rainfall evenly distributed over the growing season. Its two zones are the Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan; major states are Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan.

questions.passage: Tenzing's uncle farms in the hills of Mizoram. Every few years the family clears a fresh patch of forest, slashes and burns the vegetation, and sows cereals and other food crops to feed themselves. They work with a hoe, a dao and digging sticks, and the whole family and neighbours share the labour. They use no fertilisers and depend on the monsoon and on the natural fertility of the soil. When the soil loses its fertility, they move on and clear another patch, leaving the old one to recover through natural processes. Tenzing learns that this kind of farming has different names in different parts of India — 'Bewar' in Madhya Pradesh, 'Podu' in Andhra Pradesh and 'Kuruwa' in Jharkhand.

parts.prompt: What is this type of farming called in the north-eastern states such as Mizoram?
parts.answer: (d) — slash and burn agriculture is called jhumming in north-eastern states like Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland.

parts.prompt: Why is land productivity low in this type of farming?

parts.prompt: Why does the family shift to a fresh patch of land, and how does this help the old patch?
parts.answer: They shift when the soil fertility decreases (1 mark); leaving the old patch allows Nature to replenish its fertility through natural processes (1 mark).

questions.stem: Describe any three modes in which minerals occur, with an example of each.
questions.answer: (i) Veins and lodes: in igneous and metamorphic rocks minerals occur in cracks, crevices, faults or joints; smaller occurrences are veins and larger ones lodes; tin, copper, zinc and lead. (ii) Beds or layers: in sedimentary rocks, formed by deposition, accumulation and concentration in horizontal strata; coal and some forms of iron ore; gypsum, potash salt and sodium salt formed by evaporation in arid regions. (iii) Residual weathering: decomposition of surface rocks and removal of soluble constituents leaves a residual mass containing ores; bauxite. (iv) Placer deposits: alluvial deposits in sands of valley floors and the base of hills; gold, silver, tin, platinum. (v) Ocean waters: common salt, magnesium, bromine; manganese nodules on ocean beds.

Anthracite is the highest quality hard coal.

questions.stem: Describe the four major iron ore belts of India.
questions.answer: (1) Odisha–Jharkhand belt: high-grade hematite in the Badampahar mines in Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar districts of Odisha; in Singbhum district of Jharkhand haematite is mined at Gua and Noamundi. (2) Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur belt in Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra: very high grade hematite in the Bailadila hills of Bastar, with 14 deposits of super high grade ore that has the best physical properties for steel making; the ore is exported to Japan and South Korea via Vishakhapatnam port. (3) Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru belt in Karnataka: large reserves; the Kudremukh mines in the Western Ghats are a 100 per cent export unit and among the largest deposits in the world; ore is sent as slurry by pipeline to a port near Mangaluru. (4) Maharashtra–Goa belt: Goa and Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra; ores are not of very high quality but are efficiently exploited and exported through Marmagao port.

questions.stem: 'Energy saved is energy produced.' Explain why India needs to conserve energy and how non-conventional sources and individual citizens can help.
questions.answer: Energy is a basic requirement for economic development; agriculture, industry, transport, commercial and domestic sectors all need it, and consumption has risen steadily since Independence. India is presently one of the least energy efficient countries in the world, so a sustainable path of energy development is urgently needed; its twin planks are promotion of energy conservation and increased use of renewable sources. Non-conventional sources help: India is blessed with abundant sunlight, water, wind and biomass; solar plants will reduce rural dependence on firewood and dung cakes, conserving the environment and leaving manure for agriculture; biogas gives energy and better manure. Citizens can use public transport instead of individual vehicles, switch off electricity when not in use, use power-saving devices and use non-conventional sources of energy.

questions.passage: Natural gas is found with petroleum deposits and is released when crude oil is brought to the surface. It is used as fuel in the power sector to generate electricity, for heating in industries, as raw material in chemical, petrochemical and fertilizer industries, and increasingly as CNG for transport and PNG for cooking at home. India's major gas reserves are found in the Mumbai High and allied fields along the west coast, supplemented by finds in the Cambay basin, and new reserves have been discovered in the Krishna-Godavari basin on the east coast. The first 1,700 km long Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur cross-country pipeline, built by GAIL (India), linked Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields with fertilizer, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India. Cross-country pipelines have since grown to 18,500 km.

Land: dumping of wastes such as glass, harmful chemicals, industrial effluents, packaging, salts and garbage renders soil useless, and rainwater carries pollutants into the ground so groundwater is contaminated. questions.stem: Trace the development of the cotton textile industry in India and explain the factors behind its early location. What problem does the weaving sector face?
questions.answer: In ancient India cotton textiles were produced by hand spinning and handloom weaving; power-looms came into use after the 18th century. Traditional industries suffered a setback during the colonial period as they could not compete with mill-made cloth from England. The first successful textile mill was established in Mumbai in 1854, and the demand for cloth in the U.K. during the two world wars boosted the industry. In the early years it was concentrated in the cotton growing belt of Maharashtra and Gujarat because of raw cotton, market, transport including port facilities, labour and moist climate. The industry supports farmers, pluckers and workers in ginning, spinning, weaving, dyeing, designing, packaging and tailoring, and creates demand for chemicals, dyes, packaging and engineering. Spinning is centralised in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu while weaving is decentralised; India has world class spinning, but weaving supplies low quality fabric as it cannot use much of the high quality yarn produced in the country.
valuePoints: Handloom tradition; setback in colonial period
First successful mill in Mumbai, 1854; world wars boosted demand
Early location in Maharashtra and Gujarat: raw cotton, market, transport, port, labour, moist climate
Links with farmers and other industries
Weaving supplies low quality fabric, unable to use high quality yarn

questions.passage: NTPC is a major power providing corporation in India. It has ISO certification for EMS (Environment Management System) 14001, and it takes a proactive approach to preserving the natural environment and resources like water, oil, gas and fuels in places where it sets up power plants. It does this through optimum utilisation of equipment by adopting the latest techniques and upgrading existing equipment; minimising waste generation by maximising ash utilisation; providing green belts to nurture ecological balance; reducing environmental pollution through ash pond management, ash water recycling and liquid waste management; and ecological monitoring, reviews and on-line database management for all its power stations.

parts.prompt: NTPC holds ISO certification for which of the following?
parts.answer: (c) — NTPC has ISO certification for EMS (Environment Management System) 14001.

parts.prompt: How does NTPC minimise waste generation?
Apart from NTPC's methods, state two ways in which factories can reduce air or noise pollution.
parts.answer: Any two (1 mark each): fitting smoke stacks with electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators; using oil or gas instead of coal; fitting generators with silencers; redesigning machinery for energy efficiency and less noise; using noise-absorbing material and earplugs.
